entries.title: Books about Mesopotamia, recommended by Moudhy Al-Rashid

entries.content:
Mesopotamia, the fertile region between the Tigris and the Euphrates, is a hugely significant part of human history, yet has often been left out of the classical civilisations curriculum. Here, Moudhy Al-Rashid, author of Between Two Rivers: Ancient Mesopotamia and the Birth of History, recommends five recent books about Mesopotamia that shed light not only milestones of history, but on individual lives thousands of years ago.

Before we get to your book recommendations, can you help to clarify some of the names that crop up? How do Sumer, Akkad, Babylonia and Assyria fit in, and what time periods are we talking about?

Mesopotamia is from the Greek, “between the rivers”. It starts getting used in very early Greek sources, and then it continues to be used — by the British, not the locals — until the birth of the modern Middle East in the early 1900s. Mesopotamia is a very problematic term. Tate Paulette, in In the Land of Ninkasi, talks about how colonial the term is, but that he is going to continue to use it. I also made the same decision in my book, because it’s a convenient designation, and if you start to get more clunky then it’s harder for people to follow exactly what part of the world we’re talking about, since it covers more than one country.

When we’re talking about ancient Mesopotamia, the region we’re talking about is Iraq, parts of Syria, and parts of Turkey. It is just a region; there’s no Mesopotamian civilisation. We may refer to the Mesopotamians as a broad brushstroke way to refer to the inhabitants of the region in antiquity. The time periods covered in these books are from around 3300 BCE to around 500 BCE. Until around 2000 BCE, in the south there were the Sumerians, but there was no Sumer in the sense of a civilisation or an empire. In the north, there were the speakers of Akkadian. These are cultural or linguistic divisions, more than anything else. Then the Sumerians disappear — at least in the records, they’re probably still around — and from around 2000 BCE until 500 BCE it becomes the Babylonians in the south and Assyrians in the north. So those designations refer to different parts of the region referred to as Mesopotamia during different eras.

Thank you for that very clear summary. Can you talk a bit more about the significance of the geographical situation between the two rivers?

It’s often called the twin rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. That’s possibly because they have the same origin point in the mountains of eastern Turkey, and then they flow through Turkey, Syria, Iraq, all the way down to the Arabian or Persian Gulf. The way they would flood and retract, and the way layers of sediment piled on top of each other, created really fertile soil. It was difficult to farm because of the unpredictable flooding, but it was very productive when it was farmed successfully. So the rivers really define the region geographically, and ultimately come to shape it culturally. All the clay deposits from the rivers become the medium for writing, and become an integral way that people understand their origins in ancient Mesopotamia. In both Sumerian and later Babylonian mythology, people are created from clay, and one of the ways to describe death is to “return to clay”.

Eventually, when people learn irrigation techniques, they’re effectively controlling the flood cycles of these rivers in order to harness water a little bit more effectively and predictably. So the rivers really do have a big impact on what emerges, on how the people understood themselves, and what they were able to build. They are quite different from each other, though. The Euphrates is a lot longer, and the water flows more slowly because more of it evaporates. The Tigris is a shorter, more fast-paced river. You can think of it like a marathon versus a sprint, and they create different city life around them, and different farming techniques as well.

All the books that you’re recommending here have been published in the last few years, and your book, Between Two Rivers, came out in 2025. Is it fair to say that Mesopotamia is becoming a hot topic, and are there any particular reasons for that?

I think it’s definitely a hotter topic than it was, but not as spicy as I’d like for it to be. One way into the interest is awareness of the influence of all the cultures to the east of Greece on the development of Greek and Roman civilisation. At the same time, there is a big movement to decolonise history in educational institutions throughout the UK and America. I think a big part of that is putting ancient Mesopotamia onto the historical map. It’s three and a half thousand years of written history; that’s over half of human written history. Putting that into the history books is a hugely important step toward doing justice to those eras and to the people who are there today, who were always aware of this history and for whom this history is all around them, but also doing justice to global history by putting it back into the narrative where it always was, but was never recognised as such. I hope that people are becoming more interested in history outside of the classical civilisations that people get taught, typically, in elementary school here in the UK, for example.

Yes, which are all, of course, important and interesting and a huge part of history. But that doesn’t mean that we have to ignore anything else that happened, and how they all influenced each other.

Eckart Frahm is a professor at Yale. He writes so accessibly about a really long and complex history — we’re talking about almost fifteen hundred years of Assyrian history — and he continues to follow the history of ancient Assyria into its legacy and how it survives in later myth and legend and stories. So it’s a really big period that he manages to condense into one book, and it’s somehow not boring to follow this chronology from start to finish. One of the reasons he’s able to make this history of political and economic milestones so interesting is that he peppers it with stories of individual lives.

That’s going to be a theme across all these books: the writers make a conscious effort to bring out the stories in the cuneiform sources that are not just about kings and queens and major literary figures like Gilgamesh. It is held together by very human moments. It’s about a woman named Urkittu-hamat who, during the twilight of the Assyrian Empire, sold herself into slavery for copper instead of gold, because that is how hungry she was.

Even as an Assyriologist, I learned a lot from this book. I learned about an attempted coup on the Assyrian Empire at its height, in which a diviner named Kudurru was forced by a general into a coup against the king (diviners were very important to the king during the Assyrian Empire, because they helped with royal decision-making). These personal stories remind us that the empire was full of people no different to us. I really love this book, and I use it in a lot of my lectures.

Frahm writes that world history begins with Assyria, that it was the world’s first empire. Do you agree? I have more often seen the state founded by Sargon of Akkad referred to as the first empire.

I would agree with you. I think the idea of empire is definitely earlier than Assyria, and it could be argued, and has been argued, that Sargon is the founder of the world’s first empire. It depends on how you want to understand empire. If it has to have a really good paper trail, then the Assyrians have a much better paper trail for their empire, and we can say more definitively what that looks like than we can for the old Akkadian or Sargonic Empire. Assyria is the biggest that the world had ever seen up to that point, for better or worse. I am actually very anti-imperialism, so I don’t talk about these things as positive movements in the history of humanity, but they happened, and they were very successful. I don’t think history begins with Assyria. What counts as history? I think anything that comes before right now is history; whether it’s before writing or after writing doesn’t matter.

This book is like a seven-course meal, but I would also like to recommend an appetiser to make it easier to make sense of the rest of the meal, or you could think of it as pairing wine and cheese: Ancient Assyria: A Very Short Introduction by Karen Radner. It is really a very good introduction. She gives a bit of background on the region more broadly, and there are some images as well as maps to help.

Tate Paulette brings so many elements of food and drink to life in this book. Those are often not addressed in histories of ancient Mesopotamia, but are really interesting because they are a way into social and economic history. Who consumed beer? Who made beer? How much were they paid? How much did it cost? What were the different kinds of beers, and who had access to them? How were dates, which were more expensive, used in beer production? How does beer production change from the very early periods to the much later Neo-Babylonian periods, when you have a lot more date-based drinks, more like a wine than a beer?

Like any good Assyriologist, Paulette looks at stories of individuals, of individual brewers, starting with Kushim, from the dawn of writing. We don’t know if Kushim was a person or an institution, but Paulette takes us through all the sources about Kushim and what they tell us about how beer was made, and what the ingredients were during these really early periods. These are some of the earliest examples of writing in human history. He talks also about taverns and tavern keepers, about how many of them were women, and what the law codes say about women tavern keepers, or women of different classes entering a tavern. He talks about taverns as social institutions and liminal spaces that may have been sometimes outside of the city, and rituals involved in the business of upkeep of a tavern.

Another thing I really loved in this book, which I think other readers would also love, is that he combines quite academic analysis of the sources — which doesn’t at any point feel overly dense or heavy — with narrative walk-throughs. He’s an archaeologist. I find it difficult to wrap my head around archaeological drawings of buildings, and Paulette really brings it to life. You get a sense of who would have had access to these buildings, what that says about society at the time, as well as the buildings themselves and what it would have been like to inhabit these spaces. He does an incredible job of that, and he does it with humour. There were some bits in this book where I was laughing out loud, unexpectedly.

Did everyone in ancient Mesopotamia drink beer?

Yes, as far as we know, everyone drank beer of some kind, maybe not the finest beer that was brewed for the deities or for ritual purposes, but even children drank beer. We don’t know how alcoholic the beer was. There are administrative records, which he talks about in the book, of children of workers being given rations of beer to drink. Beer is used a lot in medical recipes, and one of the possible reasons is that it was cleaner than water. When you’re ill, when your immune system is already depressed, you don’t want to get another secondary illness from contaminated water. Beer is a safe drink, even if it is alcoholic.

And there is a hymn to Ninkasi, the goddess of beer.

Yes, and he talks about the different ways to interpret this hymn. It is essentially a step-by-step recipe of how to make beer, but we don’t understand all the terms in it because Sumerian is not fully deciphered. He goes through the different interpretations offered and suggests how it might have been carried out. The last chapter, which is great, is how they actually brewed this beer based on the recipes from ancient Mesopotamia, and got people together for ancient beer tasting. How else to know if this recipe could be feasible, without trying to do it yourself and seeing what the outcome is? I love experimental archaeology.

Podany’s book is really comprehensive, from before the birth of writing all the way to the Persians, and how life changed or didn’t change in Babylonia under the Persians. It is a really incredible book because she brings to life each era. She gives just enough historical context for you to understand the sources that she picks and chooses. This is a chronological history, and usually I find them a bit too dense and repetitive, but this one is structured around individuals, which I really love. Individual kings and queens, yes, but also abandoned children, enslaved workers who tried to run away, working mothers, men and women who made bricks in the baking sun with clay that would have been stuck in their skin… She brings it to life, and really thinks about the nitty-gritty details that aren’t in the sources, that you have to calculate through some other ways in order to bring this to life.

She gives an example, during the Early Dynastic Period — which is a huge period from around 2900 to 2300 BCE, the height of Sumerian culture — of how the most vulnerable in society, children without homes, went into a sort of care system. That often meant they were attached to different households or workplaces. I don’t want anyone to imagine that this was some utopia where children were treated amazingly, but they weren’t left behind. There’s one whose name was Putapada, which means ‘found from a well’. Podany talks about this child’s life and what we know about this child from the records. She does a really beautiful job of making it about people, but still covering a huge amount of time and giving enough information that you finish the book feeling like you know a lot.

She also answers questions that I’ve always had, for example about the very famous Assyrian palace reliefs, most of which are not in Iraq anymore. They’re incredible pieces of art, but we don’t actually know step by step how they were made. She fills in the blanks with adjacent sources on related pieces. For example, a statue was being fashioned during the Neo-Assyrian period by someone called Nabu-ashared. There are letters back and forth between this man and the king, where he shares competing ideas among different artists about how to style the work. He writes to the king with some complaints, and asks the king to tell him what he should do with the statue. I really loved that.

This book is really long, but it’s easy to follow because of the way she structures it through people’s lives and dives into details that make it so interesting. The other great thing about it is that it’s written in such a way that you can skip parts without feeling lost later down the line; it can be digested as a whole or piecemeal. But if you don’t have time or need some basics before doing a deep dive, Podany’s The Ancient Near East: A Very Short Introduction is amazing, too.

The authors of the different essays in this catalogue really let the sources speak for themselves. They guide you through it and help readers interpret some of it, but it is really a collection of what the sources say about different subjects. It feels like someone is holding your hand and walking you through these complex moments in history, giving just enough guidance for you to understand the sources and enjoy them. The stunning images stand out so much in this book, and it is really full of generous sharing of skill and knowledge, as well as of the objects themselves. There’s a wonderful chapter called ‘Number Culture: Old Babylonian Mathematics at Yale’, and some of the images are of tablets with area diagrams or other calculations that required a drawing of a spatial calculation. And there is a beautiful synopsis with incredible images of how people learned math four thousand years ago, and who learned it, so that you know what the people back then were making.

The other thing I really love about this book is that it is such a diverse sampling of topics. You have the hardcore intellectual history, like the birth of writing, Old Babylonian math, ideas about time and calendars. But you also have chapters about family life. There’s an incredible chapter about food that breaks down recipes to the point where you can make them at home. So it is a really nice melange of topics that can appeal to any reader, and you don’t have to read it from start to finish, you can just pick the ones you think are interesting. At the end, there are more pages of objects that have been referenced throughout, a catalogue of photos and descriptions of objects. It pairs image and text nicely for those who want to see the objects but can’t travel to Yale, like most people. I really love this book. I recommend it to everyone. Many of the chapters have been made publicly available, but I’m really glad that somebody gave me a hard copy to look at.

I was really fascinated by the chapter on cuneiform. Can you elaborate a bit on the birth of writing?

Yes, of course, it’s one of my favourite topics. Someone asked me on a podcast last year if people in ancient Mesopotamia knew they were on the cusp of something world-changing when they developed writing. I said, based on where these texts were found, probably not. About four thousand tablets were found in a kind of rubbish heap from the layer of archaeology just before 3200 BCE. They document the development of this technology that people needed to keep track of vast quantities of information that would be difficult to do in your head or using tokens, which had been used traditionally for a long time before writing was developed. These tokens were like little game pieces, where each one represents a certain number of a commodity. At some point, the method of containing this information moved from individual tokens to a single clay tablet with the same information traced onto it. Initially, this information — I don’t think we can call it writing — is more like a mnemonic device, a number followed by a drawing of the thing being counted.

Like an oil jar or beer jug emoji?

Exactly. And then you start to see lists of signs that were being used by the administrators in these transactional records, but also signs to try to make the information more complete. Around 2900 BCE, they stop tracing — it’s actually quite laborious — and that’s when you start to get the telltale shape of the cuneiform wedges impressed into clay, the tiny triangles with the lines, and you start to find hints at grammar. Then it just takes off from there.

Over time, how many languages were written in cuneiform?

About ten. Within the region that we call Mesopotamia, it was primarily Sumerian and Akkadian, and then later old Persian. The Hittites used it a little bit further north in what is now Turkey. Hurrian was also written in cuneiform. Ugaritic had a cuneiform-based alphabet. In Syria, Eblaite was a cuneiform language. The cuneiform writing system became quite flexible.

Who learnt to write? Did people go to school to learn to write in ancient Mesopotamia?

Writing was passed down within scholarly or scribal families. A specific subset of society got to go to school because they were connected with or part of these families. This included girls. Someone who worked in administration would have had to master the signs they needed to make everyday legal and transactional records, and the occasional calculation for the yield of a field. They would have had really good math that they learned as part of the standard curriculum. Babylonian and Assyrian scholars who did an apprenticeship with another scholar, let’s say a medical practitioner, would have had to master the entire repertoire of cuneiform signs. That is at least six hundred signs, and within each sign there are multiple meanings, some of which are syllabic sounds, some of which are words, some of which are specific combinations, and you have to pick the meaning from the context. Even if they were writing in Akkadian, they used a lot of Sumerian logograms as well. There are a lot of different meanings for each sign, and that’s a product of how the writing system developed, which itself is a very interesting history.

In a lot of periods there was functional literacy, so even if you didn’t go to school, you learned enough signs, say around one hundred, to be able to draft your own letter to a business partner or to a loved one, so that you didn’t have to pay a scribe to do it.

We have come to your final book recommendation about Mesopotamia, Enheduana: The Complete Poems of the World’s First Author, with translation and essays by Sophus Helle. I really like his version of Gilgamesh, too, and am glad you picked this book. What do you want to highlight about it?

Sophus Helle is an incredible writer and a meticulous scholar. These translations of Enheduana’s work capture what it might have felt like to read them or to listen to them in the original. The poetry is so impactful and so breathtaking, and he does such a great job of striking a balance between fidelity and poetry. It’s just gorgeous, I don’t know how he does it. He includes some essays on Enheduana herself, her historical context, and the textual history of the work. These are also beautifully written and readable; somehow, even his academic writing is quite poetic, and it offers a window onto the world before you immerse yourself into the poetry.

One thing that I really love about this book is that somebody with absolutely no knowledge of Sumerian, of Enheduana, of the Sargonic Empire, of cuneiform, of Mesopotamia, someone who’s never heard of any of these things, can pick this book up and A) read it with ease and enjoy the beauty of his language, and B) really get a sense of this world by the end of it. He opens it up to so many people, which is wonderful. I really love his work. Enheduana is the earliest writer whose name we know.

There is some argument about whether she really composed the poems, because the earliest extant versions are from several centuries after her lifetime. Can you shed any light on the argument for or against the historicity of her authorship?

I think it’s interesting to complicate her authorship of the poems without necessarily concluding at the end that she didn’t author them, because I don’t think that’s where these arguments have to lead. There are other ways to interpret the evidence. As far as I know, all Sumerian literature is only known from later copies made in schools by Babylonian students learning the Sumerian language. The idea of an original is a difficult question in and of itself. There was a practice of crediting well-known historical figures with authorship to lend credibility to a piece of work. I don’t know that this is an argument against her authorship; it might also be an argument for saying that they’re crediting her because she actually wrote them.

Helle makes the point that, unlike hymns that were written in the names of later kings, these poems are soul-searching and poetically pathbreaking. Their purpose was to help keep people safe from the violent whims of the gods, by invoking the gods and enlisting their help. Can you talk a bit about that?

What I think is interesting about Enheduana’s hymns is that although she was high priestess to the moon god Nanna (that’s the Sumerian name, Sin is the Akkadian name), many of her hymns are about Inanna, the goddess of love and war — Ishtar in Babylonian and Assyrian pantheons. She extols this goddess’ power in a way that is surprisingly graphic at times. It’s different, definitely, to other hymns that are quite formulaic.

I do think that there is a power that she talks about in her poetry that beautifully captures what people can and can’t have control over in their lives, that they are at the mercy of the divine, or what they understood as the divine. There’s no distinction in the terminology for ancient Mesopotamia between a phenomenon and the deity responsible for the phenomenon. There is no other way to refer to the moon other than by the name of the moon god. There is no way to refer to the sun except by the name of the sun god. I think there was a real sense that these divine beings were not separate from the world, they were the world. They were in control of the climate, of the harvest. Whether people lived or died was at the mercy of these phenomena, and these phenomena were the deities responsible for them. That power is captured really beautifully in Enheduana’s poems.

Enheduana was a priestess, and rituals would be very important in that role. How important were rituals to people in Mesopotamia in general, do we know?

I think they were very important. A ritual is a kind of expression of one’s connection with the phenomena I was just talking about. It’s a way to feel some kind of control over — or participation in — these phenomena that people relied on for their survival. I also think rituals are ways for people to come together. We still do these, it’s a really human thing. At my college, for example, there is a Christmas tree lighting ceremony. I take my kids every year, even though we’re not Christian, because it’s not a religious ceremony, it’s just such a nice thing in the community to be a part of, especially when it’s dark and rainy and there’s a bit of light there, and a reminder that these are people that you might be able to rely on if you need to.

I think that the priestess, in leading these rituals, had a very important role that transcended a symbolic figurehead. This was really deeply important to the people of Ur where Enheduana was the high priestess; an important part of their marking the seasons, an important part of their hoping for a successful harvest in a climate that was oscillating between flood levels of rain and scorching heat. These were important things that she presided over, and it would have involved quite a lot of practice and training. That was in addition to her administrative role as a priestess, because the temple owned lots of property, including agricultural property, so she would have had a lot of hats to wear within that role that was not just ritual-based, but that ritual was a big part of.

What do we know about how the ancient Mesopotamians saw themselves? What was their relationship with the wider world? Did they write about other people and other lands?

There were vast connections between people in the heartland of what we would call Mesopotamia, and people exterior to that. There were periods of international trade, like the old Assyrian period from around 1900 to 1600 BCE, when primarily women living in Assur were weaving textiles that must have been really something, because of the prices they were fetching in a trading post called Kanesh, in what is now Turkey. There is definitely a sense of a different place with different practices and different people that they found ways to interact with in a peaceful way. And we see linguistic hints at trade; how the word for horse, for example, migrates from the beginning of horse trading. So I think there’s definitely knowledge of them being in a much wider world.

There are also terms for self, for individual. There’s a word ‘ramanu’, which means self or soul. There is a sense of the individual and its place in a wider nexus of divine and human and animal and natural world, and how to mediate all those different relationships. There are so many different ways to answer that question, it’s a great question. Of course, we’re talking about three thousand years of history, so someone in 2800 BCE would answer the question very differently to someone in 538 BCE, when Cyrus arrives from Persia and takes over Babylon. And a king might answer very differently to Putapada, who was found in a well and incorporated into a workforce so that he wasn’t left on his own. It’s a very rich question.

We have barely touched on science. Can you talk a little bit about the development of science in Mesopotamia?

From the earliest writing in ancient Mesopotamia, you can find attempts to bring order to what, as we all know, is a chaotic world. Even the early lists that are arranged thematically that generate signs for writing is an attempt at completeness. We might not approach it in the same way, but that systematisation, that way of thinking scientifically about the world is there from a very early period.

There are also very early records of how regularly they were making observations of the natural world, whether it was the human body or the skies. They were almost obsessively observant, so much so that they were able to predict cyclical phenomena, astronomical phenomena, for example, or distinguish between different types of seizures, whether epileptic or not. Part of the reason for this was because anything could be a divine message.

I think they were doing science very early in very interesting ways, and if we approach it without anachronism, as people trying to make sense of the world around them in a systematic way, then we can add so much to the history of science from the cuneiform sources.

Thank you very much for introducing these fascinating books about Mesopotamia to our readers. By the way, I really enjoyed your own book Between Two Rivers and the way it’s concerned with people’s lives. I particularly loved the description of bricks with dog paw prints and clay writing tablets with children’s fingerprints from thousands of years ago.

Five Books aims to keep its book recommendations and interviews up to date. If you are the interviewee and would like to update your choice of books (or even just what you say about them) please email us at [email protected]

Five Books interviews are expensive to produce. If you've enjoyed this interview, please support us by donating a small amount.

Moudhy Al-Rashid

Moudhy Al-Rashid is an Honorary Fellow of Wolfson College, University of Oxford, where she specialises in the languages and history of ancient Mesopotamia. She teaches Akkadian texts and the history of science in Mesopotamia, and regularly appears on podcasts.

entries.title: The best books on Knitting, recommended by Rosie Fletcher
entries.summary: Knitting provides a slow, screen-free creative outlet, and opens up a wealth of style choices that you can’t buy on the high street. We asked the author and knitting teacher Rosie Fletcher to recommend five knitting books to take you from total beginner to jumper enthusiast, via troubleshooting manuals, easy-knit projects, stitch dictionaries, and vintage patterns. This interview appeared first on
entries.content:
Knitting is hugely popular. In a world where we can buy all the knitted goods we want, why take up knitting?

Number one, it’s really fun! The world is very digital, very screen based, and knitting is an incredible thing you can do that doesn’t require a screen. It’s very slow, and that is one of the good things about it! Once you’ve knitted a scarf or a jumper or even a little square, you realise how long it would take to make a jumper that you’d buy in a shop, and you get this incredible instant appreciation for creativity, for labour, for clothing… Knitting opens your eyes to a whole world. And it’s fun, and you get to play with colour and shapes and creativity, and it’s meditative – and it’s the best, basically.

Great. I thought we’d say a little about your own book first, since this is a book for the very beginning: You Will Be Able To Knit By The End Of This Book.

I often say the title is not legally binding! The idea of this book is that you can start here, from having never touched knitting needles before. The first half is how to do it, from literally what needles are, and how you match your wool with your needles; and it takes you through to actually knitting, adding more complicated steps. Then there are 16 patterns for projects in there that build you up from the most basic thing you could make, to still-super-accessible but more elaborate things.

Amazing! Do you teach people to knit, yourself?

Yes, one of my main jobs is I’m a knitting teacher. It’s really fun. At the start of the class, one thing I always say is: you’re not allowed to not enjoy it! Or if you don’t enjoy knitting, you’ve got to wait ’til you leave the shop to tell…

I’ve taught loads of people. I’ve been teaching for about seven years, and I teach all sorts of things, absolute beginners and more advanced stuff. The beginners class is three hours, and the first hour can be summarised by the fact that fifty per-cent of the time, at least one person says, ‘I thought this was meant to be relaxing.’ The second hour is when everyone gets it, but they’re very quiet: there’s a lot of concentration. And then by the third hour, everyone’s knitting away and chatting. I can almost set my watch by it.

Great! So our imagined knitter can now knit. They can pick up the first of your five choices: 52 Weeks Of Easy Knits.

This is part of a whole series from Laine called ’52 Weeks’.

Picking five books was not an easy task for me – there are a lot of knitting books, and it’s quite a personal thing – but I went for books that I thought would be generally very useful. A lot of people learn to knit, and they maybe make a scarf, then think: Now I’ve got the basics, where do I begin? And they’ll pick up a really complicated cable jumper pattern… Maybe there should be a step between the scarf and the fisherman’s sweater.

I love this book. It has 52 patterns for that stage: now you’ve learnt the basics, where to go from there? The jumper on the front is basically four squares of knit – I don’t think you even have to purl…

For any readers who don’t know, there are two basic knitting stitches, right?

Yes. There is what’s called ‘knit’ or ‘plain’, and ‘purl.’ They are basically the same stitch, looking from different sides. My analogy is always that if I were writing on a window so that you could read it from the outside, I’d have to write the letter backwards: that’s what a purl is. It’s doing the knit stitch backwards.

When I first saw this book, I thought, “Dang, I want to knit that jumper.” And I don’t need easy knits! It’s really good. They’re really modern, it’s £20, and you get 52 patterns, which is incredible value.

What’s in there?

There are lots of different things: jumpers, hats, scarves… I think there are socks in there. There’s a snood, there’s a hood, there are shawls; there are cardigans and vests and mittens. A range of things!

Okay, so our imagined knitter has been working their way through 52 Weeks Of Easy Knits, but they’re coming across problems. So let’s turn to your next choice: Patty Lyons’ Knitting Bag of Tricks.

So this is not really a how to knit for beginners, although obviously it will tell you how to do things. It is really about troubleshooting, and that is a huge part of knitting. People get put off when they know enough to know that something’s wrong, but they don’t know why it’s wrong, or what’s wrong, or how it’s wrong, or how to how to fix it. I was trying to divide the five books up: obviously your beginner book will be my book, then easy knit, then troubleshooting.

There are little illustrations explaining, for example, why your knitting is too tight or too loose. If your knitting is too loose, you have to size your needle size down, but it can get a bit like that meme of the woman with the maths around her: you’re counting your stitches, and you’re meant to have twenty stitches in this four-inch section, and you’ve got fifteen… I love that it explains all that in a very accessible, illustrated way. And there’s a sense of humour to it, which I really appreciate.

As a knitting teacher for beginners, people often ask me how I got good. I say, well, I was bad for a very long time. The way you get good is by being bad, but then being able to fix what you did wrong, and I think a book like this is an amazing resource to have on hand.

We’ve mentioned knitting too tight or loose – what are the other most common stumbling blocks for beginner knitters?

The main one is thinking it’s going to be right first time. People in classes will say, ‘Mine doesn’t look like yours!’ – and I say, ‘I hope it doesn’t, because this is my job.’ You’ve got to let it be bad, which is a mindset thing more than a technique thing.

The other is not being able to read what you did in the previous row. That’s when you are doing something where you have to, say, alternate between different stitches, and you put it down and pick it up again, and think, ‘What the heck did I do in the previous row?’ Being able to tell what you did is a really integral thing.

Great. Your next choice is intriguing: tell us about Jamie Lomax’s The Doodle Knitting Card Deck.

I wanted to include a stitch dictionary of some kind. Stitch dictionaries are what they sound like: they are a collection of different stitches that you might use – because although there are basically only two, the combinations you put them in make all the elaborate patterns you can imagine. High street jumpers are all made up from how you combine very basic stitches.

This is presented as a deck. There’s been a huge trend in the craft world for card decks, which started with the Granny Square Card Deck – I couldn’t include that because it’s crochet, but we have to give a little tip of the hat to that one. The Doodle cards are by the designer Jamie Lomax, and she has been doing these for ages. They are really great colourwork patterns, which are just combinations of different colours to make very cute, fun motifs – she calls them doodles. Each card has the basics: they look like little graphs you could literally use excel to make them, with cells filled in with colour. And on the back, there’s a photo of what it looks like knitted up.

There are loads of different stitch dictionaries: you can get colourwork and you can get texture, and you can combine the two. But this one is very much my style and it’s very on trend.

There are some beautifully elaborate looking ‘doodles.’ They look really impressive.

Yeah, I just like the style! Obviously the content is good, but something about the style and her eye for design, and the colours she uses, are also just very appealing. And how nice to have a little tactile thing, and to rummage through all the little cards to pick out a design.

Very appealing. Ok, we’ve come to your fourth choice – the third volume of A Stitch In Time by Sarah Crawford.

Knitting is hundreds of years old, but people really associate it with mid-twentieth century – the 1920s, 1930s, and 1940s. If I see one more thing saying, ‘knitting is not just for grandmas,’ I will explode, because people have been saying that since the early noughties revival of knitting. The people you were saying that about twenty years ago could be well on their way to being grandmas by now!

Knitting is a very modern thing. But at the same time, I do love that mid-twentieth century knitted look, and I think it draws a lot of people in: they see these styles that you can’t buy on the high street, and there are knitting patterns for clothes that you can’t buy anymore.

Crawford has taken vintage designs and patterns, and made them size inclusive and accessible. If you’ve ever tried to look at an actual knitting pattern from the 1940s, you’ll know it is an A5 piece of paper, and you need a magnifying glass; you will be a size six, that’s the only option; you can follow them, but they’re written in a different way. This book expands those instructions, and also literally expands the sizing, to make these vintage patterns actually accessible to modern knitters.

I can read those old-style knitting patterns, but I do find myself thinking, what if we used a whole word rather than everything being abbreviated?

This blows my mind! The only patterns I have ever tried were my granny’s, and they were all abbreviations. I can have patterns in full English?

Yes! There’s one designer called PetiteKnit who was incredibly popular, with lovely, quite basic ideas that were really well executed. She writes her patterns basically in full sentences. For me that was probably a bit much, but other people love it.

This book is about colourwork. Colourwork is using multiple colours of wool at the same time to make up a pattern. The example I always use is the jumper from The Killing, with the snowflake design – that’s colourwork. Or those classic multicoloured, stripy 1930s and 1940s tank tops, which you can knit from this book – that’s colourwork. It’s often called ‘Fair Isle,’ but I believe it’s a bit like champagne – if it’s not from Fair Isle, itself it’s just sparkling colour work. So this volume is all about using multiple colours to make that really classic vintage look, and I love it.

Wonderful. Your last choice sounds like it may be a real best-loved book for you: this is The Beatrix Potter Knitting Book.

This is slightly a stand-in for all charity shop knitting book finds, but this is my all-time favourite of those. We were talking about the history of knitting and how it’s still a very modern craft, but there is something special for people of my age – firmly millennial – about licensed knitting books with beloved characters.

There’s a technique for knitting blocks of colour in your knitting called ‘intarsia’; when people ask what it is, I say, imagine the jumper that has Postman Pat on the front. That’s intarsia – using blocks of colour to make a picture. I found this Beatrix Potter one in a charity shop, and I adore it. It is spectacularly 1980s. You can find these for loads of stuff, these tie-in books, but I think this one’s really good. I was going to say the designs don’t age, but then look at this Edwardian lace girl smock…

I just love this book, and when I find old knitting books in charity shops, I am an absolute sucker for them.

I would wear one item in this, which is the design on the cover, from The Tailor of Gloucester. You know the story, where he’s making a waistcoat for the mayor? They’ve made the design that he’s embroidering in that story into a knitting chart for your colourwork! I might apply that design to a less mid-1980s style, but it’s really fun to find inspiration all over the place with knitting.

Yes – that’s where it can get really creative.

As I said, it’s how you can make clothes that you can’t find in the shops, whether that’s based on the design, the fit, the fibre content – and that gives you an appreciation for what clothing and textiles can be made of. They are not going to sell you these items on the high street. And that’s fair; if your friend was having a baby and you knitted them one of these they would be very touched, but they might also say, ‘Why have you knitted me this Squirrel Nutkin fuzzy hat and coat?’

There’s such a wealth of knowledge in knitting books, and they are also hilariously kitsch. I just love having this on my shelf.

And it’s so great to be able to open up all those clothing styles we’ve just quietly dropped.

I know I’m here to talk about books, but let me be evangelical for a moment about making your own things! I am hugely concerned with the environmental impact of fashion. When you have made something with your hands and you realise how long it takes, and you then remember that all clothing is handmade – they have knitting machines, but the sewing up of things is still done by individuals. Then you go onto the high street and you think: ‘How is that eight pounds?’ If I bought the fibre or the wool for it, it would be more than eight pounds, and then it would take hours to knit it. Obviously if it’s machine knitted that’s faster, but still.

So then you start asking: ‘Who is getting exploited?’ I think it might be everyone at every step of the chain. Then you buy these things and they fall apart, they don’t fit, and they don’t breathe because they’re plastic.

When you make something slowly you can make it in natural fibres, which are more expensive, but I’ve got really into thrifting and using second-hand marketplaces like Vinted, where there are so many knitting and sewing supplies. Plus, projects take forever, so as a cost-per-hour hobby, knitting is incredibly cheap!

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

entries.title: Five Funny Sci Fi Books, recommended by Andrew Hunter Murray
entries.summary: Sci fi with a touch of humour can help us explore the oddities of existence, argues bestselling author Andrew Hunter Murray. He picks five books that made him laugh, from dystopias to outer space to crime thrillers, each with a unique perspective to make us chuckle – sometimes at ourselves. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
What were your criteria for choosing these five books?

It’s simply that they made me laugh. They’re all very different, and they all have very different ways of making me laugh.

Let’s talk about your first choice: The Hopkins Manuscript, by R. C. Sherriff.

The Hopkins Manuscript is a very prescient bit of sci fi from 1939. The premise is simple: the moon is going to crash into the Earth. That’s a very serious situation, and the only reason this book is a comedy in most part is because of the narrator. He is a well-meaning amateur astronomer who is more interested in raising prized chickens than in the end of the world as it’s approaching. It’s basically the apocalypse, as told by Alan Partridge. By a quirk of his hobby, his interest in astronomy, he is one of a very select band of people who know the horrible truth – that the moon is about to crash into the Earth – before anyone else does.

Having a strong character makes the difference between a brilliant comedy and a bad one. He’s so funny, and he’s so well-meaning – he’s a very small-minded and petty person, but he’s not malign. He’s quite benevolent in general. When the moon does crash into the earth, and there’s a requirement to rebuild civilization afterwards, he comes out of his shell a bit and becomes a bit less of a difficult and annoying character.

It’s a wonderful and weird premise, and it was written right on the eve of the Second World War. And there is a strain in it towards the end about the folly and the horror of war, where it does become a bit more serious.

I think another element that’s important for a comic novel is that it has to reflect human nature, which is basically unchanging: the circumstances can change, but human nature doesn’t. That’s always one of my rules for writing fiction.

So that’s the story of Hopkins and his manuscript, and I just adore it.

Why ‘manuscript’? Is it supposed to be an old document?

Yes. There is a little foreword from the Imperial Research Press in Addis Ababa, so it has this lovely little framing device: it’s been tracked down centuries after it was written. The idea is we’re well into the future, and the Royal Society of Abyssinia discovered the Hopkins manuscript two years ago in the ruins of Notting Hill. It was hoped that some valuable light would be at last thrown upon the final tragic days of London – but, it says, unfortunately Edgar Hopkins is so self-regarding, vain, and useless as a narrator that his narrative is almost valueless. I really love that too, as a way of saying, ‘You’re not going to get anything useful out of this story.’

It’s so funny. R.C. Sherriff was a brilliant writer, and a very varied one in his career. He wrote A Fortnight in September, which is literally just about a family going on holiday for a fortnight in September… So he could do very big stuff and very small stuff at the same time, and all of it manages to engage the reader. He’s terrific.

He was writing this in 1939, of course, but dystopian collapse doesn’t feel far away today either… Is it a stressful read?

No, I don’t think so. It’s such a warm and funny book, and the idea of the moon deciding to spiral in and crash into the Earth is so absurd that I don’t think it is stressful to read. It’s quite encouraging to read in a way – chicken breeding goes on, even under the most difficult circumstances.

That is comforting. Great, could you tell us about your second choice? This is Jasper Fforde’s The Eyre Affair.

This is the story of Tuesday Next, who is a literary detective. She lives in an alternate reality where reading is much more core to day-to-day life than it is in our own world, and the plot concerns the abduction of Jane Eyre from her own book.

Tuesday Next is a detective who can move between books. So can the villains of the piece. The whole thing is just completely wonderful. If you’re a fan of reading, it’s wonderful, not least because there are a vast number of references to other works of fiction scattered through the pages. But you don’t have to have read everything to enjoy The Eyre Affair and all of its sequels (Tuesday Next crops up in lots more books).

There’s something about the sheer pleasure in reading and the joy of the world that Jasper Fforde creates that makes it very infectious. It’s a wild story as well, and you’re able to pinwheel through all sorts of different worlds. I don’t know if Jasper Fforde would like the comparison, but I thought it was like a much, much more sophisticated version of Ready Player One, which borrows from all sorts of other fictional worlds. But because Jasper Fforde was doing it with literature, and because he was doing it first, I think it is better on both counts.

Pinwheeling is a great description. It’s definitely sci fi, but it’s also fantasy, and it’s also police procedural… Do you feel one genre has the dominant note, or is it just its own thing?

It’s so mad – I remember there’s a scene where there’s a kind of mass Richard III, almost a sing-along Richard III, where everyone’s quoting along to the entire play… I think it’s a bit of everything. I do like a detective novel because they have so much potential for comedy. Again, because there’s such a strong narrative voice – which we’re probably going to come onto with one of the upcoming choices…

Let’s talk about that one now then. What is Titanium Noir by Nick Harkaway about?

It’s so good. It’s about a gumshoe detective called Cal Sounder, who lives in a world of giants. A technology has been invented which, after the first injection, makes you 20% taller, younger, and harder to kill. There are only about two thousand of these Titans on the planet, but they control almost everything, and the people who’ve taken three or four doses are now absolutely enormous and absolutely impossible to kill.

Cal Sounder is a human who works as a kind of fixer for these titans, and this is a crime story he gets caught up in, where the victim is himself a titan: seven feet tall and ninety years old, but doesn’t look a day over thirty. Since titans being killed is impossible, Cal Sounder has to investigate just exactly what has happened.

And he’s the main vehicle for the comedy?

Yes – this is another one which is so character-led. The character of the gumshoe detective is such a well-established one. But this crazy world of near-future titans and genetic manipulation allows Harkaway to have a huge amount of fun with that, and to be very world-weary about a grubby, Blade Runner-style broken world.

It’s not actually a comedy. This is probably the least out-and-out funny of the five I’ve chosen. But it did make me laugh a lot. There are a lot of scenes which are very funny because the main character is funny, and that does almost all the work for you. So you’re laughing throughout, even though you don’t realise you are.

I know we’re here to discuss funny sci fi, but you do also write funny crime – and there’s so much of it about. Is there something about the crime novel that lends itself to humour?

It doesn’t have to, because there are a lot of extremely serious crime novels. This all links to: what makes things funny? I’ve been thinking about comedy and satire a lot recently, and whether satire has to have a joke in it. I used to think it did, but I now believe I was wrong. Actually, all you need is a perspective, a changed outlook on the world that you’re trying to communicate to your audience. I think that’s all comedy really needs: to present a different way of looking at the world. The classic form is a joke, where there’s a bit of a surprise in it. But the reason that character comedy is so strong is because an individual, a well-written character, can have a completely different perspective on the world. If you can write a character whose perspective is consistent and different to most other people’s, comedy is the inevitable result.

Detective stories also rely to a large extent on strong characters. The crime may not be especially interesting, but your detective will certainly have to be. Look at stories like the Lord Peter Wimsey mysteries, where he’s a cricket-playing aristocrat who has decided to quixotically go around solving crimes more for his own amusement than anything else: that’s a terrific character, and he’s such a weird character that he can’t help being funny, just because he’s different to all of us.

Interesting. So, you’ve written funny crime, and you’ve written sci-fi, but your next book brings together the humour and the sci fi for the first time. Tell us about Everything Happens So Much.

It’s about a woman called Esme Good. Esme has a job she doesn’t like, and a life she doesn’t really like – she’s never quite managed to get into gear. That’s her basic problem. Part of the reason for that is that she is addicted to a little substance called the Elsewheres. The Elsewheres are a technology that you can take a dose of, in a pill or potion or whatever it might be, and for fifteen minutes you are catapulted into the mind of one of the other versions of you, one of the other trillions of versions of you that might have been. Esme really, really likes these things, and she has spent so many years in other versions of her own head that she has completely failed to start living her own life.

It’s basically a book about the experience of being alive now, and why it feels so difficult to thrive and simply get on with one’s own life – because we’re bombarded with everyone else’s lives constantly. It’s really about the twenty years since social media was invented in a big way.

Esme goes through an experience, which means that she is forced to start living her own life. She actually becomes an immensely important person – and she doesn’t handle it very well. So that’s the setup. There’s a huge caper adventure that rolls out from there.

This is the book I’ve been writing for – gosh, about ten years now. – working on it and improving it. Again it’s character-led.

A real labour of love. What have you discovered from the process of bringing humour and sci fi together?

In both sci fi and humour, I like work that – as we’ve touched on – reflects reality and human nature. I think there are some sci fi works in the space opera category, which have a little too much sci fi for me, and not quite enough of the human behaviour. The really successful works are those which combine them. This kind of sci fi works for me because we’re in a recognisable version of our world – it just happens that things go a bit crazy.

At the same time, the fact that you’re in a world where things are allowed to be different means that you can do all sorts of things, and the only limit is your imagination, which is so enjoyable. It’s so nice spending time in a book that an author has really thought about, and where they’ve shown you little touches of the world without having to go into huge detail – and that again can be a huge vehicle for comedy. So that’s why the combination works.

It’s time for your fourth choice: “Sell Out,” which is a short story in Simon Rich’s collection, Spoiled Brats (and was serialised in The New Yorker).

Yes. This is the story of Herschel Greenbaum, a worker at a pickle factory in 19th-century New York, who falls into a big vat of pickles and is frozen there for over a century – until he’s thawed out, returned to life, and goes to meet his great-great-grandson. Simon Rich has been a writer on SNL for many years, and he writes fantastic short story collections.

It’s a classic mismatched pair comedy. The story is told from the perspective of the great-great-grandfather. He starts selling his own pickles on the streets of New York using river water, completely unsanitary pickles, and is shocked when he’s stopped from doing this – a classic fish out of water story. And he’s convinced that his great-great -grandson and his great-great-grandson’s girlfriend are doing terribly badly for themselves because they’re so thin; he’s worried that they’re going to starve, because that was much more of a concern in Eastern Europe in the 19th century, where he came from.

It’s an extremely funny story. Simon Rich is so good at creating little worlds, quite economically, yet stuffed with brilliant observation. It was done as a film with Seth Rogen, which is a very good low-budget comedy film of the kind that you don’t really get many of these days. It’s good, and worth watching, but the story is even better.

We spoke about satire – some of these jabs are pretty sharp, and aimed squarely at the average New Yorker reader. And at me, honestly, but it didn’t feel bad to laugh at them…

No, it’s fine. The character of the great-great-grandson is quite clearly based on Simon Rich himself, because he’s a comedy writer who is working on punching up incredibly stupid-sounding comedy scripts, like one where the president is a monkey… So he’s having a go at himself.

It’s part of a short story collection called Spoiled Brats, which begins with a harrowing gulag-style memoir by a class hamster. They’re not all sci fi, but they all have an amazing way of presenting perspectives.

Being funny in short story form must be a different art…

Yes. It’s how I started, before novels. I wrote a lot of short stories, which were sci fi and comic, very much in the Douglas Adams mould. You’re allowed to be a bit madder in them, because you don’t have to sustain a serious story over 100,000 words. In fact –  and I know we’re about to come on to it – the books in the Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy series are almost a collection of short stories strung together. Douglas Adams will just go off and tell a five-hundred-word story about a particular planet or civilization or technology, and then drop back into the main narrative. It’s a way of sneaking in a lot of extra crunchy detail, which is always fun.

Yes – the time has come, let’s talk about Douglas Adams. Of course his Hitchhiker’s Guide series is on your list – but you’ve specifically chosen the fourth of the trilogy of four (which would eventually become five). This is So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish. Can a reader start the series here?

Definitely read the rest of the series first. That’s no imposition. They’re all about 40,000 words long – they’re so short. I’m shocked by how short they are, given how much they do with their word count, and how big an impact they’ve had on my life.

This is the book in the Hitchhiker’s series where Arthur Dent falls in love, with a girl called Fenchurch. It’s 42 years this year since it came out…

Aha. “42”, we should explain, is an important number in the Hitchhiker’s world – it’s the answer to the ultimate question.

Yes. There isn’t a huge amount of sci fi in this story. There’s a little plot, but not an enormous one. It’s a really beautiful story about falling in love and learning to fly, and there isn’t a huge threat to the universe – no evil army to be defeated. But it’s about the change in your perspective when you fall in love, and the fact that it is almost a sci fi experience in itself, to really fall for someone. It’s a really charming and beautiful story, with lots of classic Douglas Adams touches, but it’s quite different to lots of the other Hitchhiker’s books.

One thing that science fiction and comedy do very well when they’re combined is to suggest why life feels the way it does, which is what I try and do in all my stuff – try and get to the heart of the human experience, and why it’s so strange and mad, and why we spend so many of our days quite stressed and unhappy when actually a lot of us are leading quite good lives by any objective standard. Sci fi can allow you to get into some of those questions.
